seeds.title: Nicomachus's theorem: the sum of the first n cubes is the n-th triangular number squared
seeds.statement: The sum of the first n cubes equals the square of the n-th triangular number: 1^3 + 2^3 + ... + n^3 = (1 + 2 + ... + n)^2 = T(n)^2, where T(n) = n(n+1)/2. This identity is called Nicomachus's theorem after Nicomachus of Gerasa, who noted the underlying odd-number decomposition at the end of Chapter 20 of his Introduction to Arithmetic (c. 100 CE). It is a checkable arithmetic identity, not folklore, and the checker VERIFIES it by directly summing the cubes and comparing to T(n)^2 for every n in a range.
seeds.source_citation: Nicomachus of Gerasa (c. 60-120 CE), Introduction to Arithmetic (Arithmetike eisagoge), ch. 20 - the identity sum of the first n cubes = (n-th triangular number)^2, 'Nicomachus's theorem'. Weisstein, 'Nicomachus's Theorem', Wolfram MathWorld; Wikipedia 'Squared triangular number'; OEIS A000537 (0,1,9,36,100,225,... = sum of first n cubes = squared triangular numbers).
seeds.author: Nicomachus of Gerasa

verification.method: Python-verified: running sum of k^3 equals T(n)^2 for every n from 1 to 20000 (0 counterexamples). Identity name + Nicomachus's Introduction to Arithmetic ch. 20 attribution confirmed against Wikipedia 'Squared triangular number' and MathWorld 'Nicomachus's Theorem' (web-checked 2026-07-04); OEIS A000537 membership (0,1,9,36,100,225,441,...) matches T(n)^2.

seeds.title: Every hexagonal number is a triangular number: H(n) = T(2n-1)
seeds.statement: Every hexagonal number is also a triangular number. The n-th hexagonal number H(n) = n(2n-1) equals the (2n-1)-th triangular number: H(n) = T(2n-1), since n(2n-1) = (2n-1)(2n)/2. Thus 1, 6, 15, 28, 45, ... (hexagonals) is a subsequence of 1, 3, 6, 10, 15, 21, 28, ... (triangulars). This is a classical figurate-number identity from the Greek arithmetic tradition (Nicomachus; Diophantus's On Polygonal Numbers), and the checker VERIFIES it by computing both H(n) and T(2n-1) for every n in a range.
seeds.canonical_statement: H(n) = n(2n-1) = T(2n-1) for all n >= 1
seeds.source_citation: Classical figurate-number theory (Nicomachus of Gerasa, Introduction to Arithmetic, c. 100 CE; Diophantus, On Polygonal Numbers, c. 250 CE) - every hexagonal number is triangular, H(n) = T(2n-1). Weisstein, 'Hexagonal Number', Wolfram MathWorld; ProofWiki 'Hexagonal Number is Triangular Number'; OEIS A000384 (hexagonal: 0,1,6,15,28,45,...) is a subsequence of A000217 (triangular).
seeds.author: Nicomachus / Diophantus

verification.method: Python-verified: H(n) = n(2n-1) equals T(2n-1) for every n from 1 to 20000 (0 counterexamples). seeds.title: Every square is the sum of two consecutive triangular numbers: n^2 = T(n-1) + T(n)
seeds.statement: Every perfect square is the sum of two consecutive triangular numbers: n^2 = T(n-1) + T(n), where T(k) = k(k+1)/2 and T(0) = 0. This follows because T(n-1) + T(n) = (n-1)n/2 + n(n+1)/2 = n^2. The relation is a staple of the classical figurate-number tradition (Theon of Smyrna; Nicomachus), often shown by arranging two triangular arrays into a square. The checker VERIFIES it by computing n^2 and T(n-1)+T(n) for every n in a range.
seeds.canonical_statement: n^2 = T(n-1) + T(n) for all n >= 1
seeds.source_citation: Classical figurate-number theory (Theon of Smyrna, c. 100 CE; Nicomachus of Gerasa, Introduction to Arithmetic, c. 100 CE) - a square is the sum of two consecutive triangular numbers, T(n-1)+T(n) = n^2. Weisstein, 'Triangular Number', Wolfram MathWorld; OEIS A000290 (squares) as sums of consecutive terms of A000217 (triangular).
seeds.author: Theon of Smyrna / Nicomachus

seeds.title: Pell equation x^2 - N*y^2 = 1: the fundamental solution from the continued fraction of sqrt(N)
seeds.statement: For a positive non-square integer N, the equation x^2 - N*y^2 = 1 (the 'Pell equation') has infinitely many integer solutions, all powers of a single fundamental (smallest) solution, which is read off the continued-fraction expansion of sqrt(N). Brahmagupta gave the composition ('bhavana') identity for combining solutions in his Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 CE), and Bhaskara II's chakravala (cyclic) method (c. 1150 CE) solved it in general - famously producing x = 1766319049, y = 226153980 for N = 61. The name 'Pell equation' is a historical misnomer (see pell-name-misnomer). The checker COMPUTES the fundamental solution via the sqrt(N) continued fraction and VERIFIES x^2 - N*y^2 = 1 exactly.
seeds.canonical_statement: fundamental (x,y) of x^2 - N*y^2 = 1 via the sqrt(N) continued fraction; x^2 - N*y^2 = 1
seeds.source_citation: Brahmagupta, Brahmasphutasiddhanta (628 CE) - the composition/bhavana identity for x^2 - N*y^2 = 1; Bhaskara II, Bijaganita (c. 1150 CE) - the chakravala (cyclic) method, which gives x=1766319049, y=226153980 for N=61. Weisstein, 'Pell Equation', Wolfram MathWorld; MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Pell's equation' (St Andrews).
seeds.author: Brahmagupta / Bhaskara II

verification.method: Python-verified: the fundamental solution from the sqrt(N) continued fraction satisfies x^2 - N*y^2 = 1 exactly (BigInt) for N=2,3,5,6,7,13,61,109,149,421,661,991; N=61 -> (1766319049, 226153980), matching the solution Bhaskara II reported. Brahmagupta-628 / Bhaskara-chakravala attribution + the N=61 figure confirmed against MacTutor 'Pell's equation' and MathWorld 'Pell Equation' (web-checked 2026-07-04).

seeds.title: Figurate numbers carry mystical / 'sacred geometry' significance - speculative LEAP
seeds.statement: That hexagonal numbers are triangular, that the sum of the first n cubes is a square, and that a square splits into two consecutive triangulars are real, checkable arithmetic facts. The further claim that figurate numbers - the Pythagorean tetractys, 'sacred' triangular or hexagonal forms - carry cosmic, divine or mystical significance (e.g. Iamblichus's Theology of Arithmetic, c. 300 CE, on the mystical potency of the tetractys and the decad) is a numerological/theological interpretation, not mathematics. It has no mathematical content beyond the figurate identities and NO promotion path to 'established'. M8 verifies the arithmetic and must label any 'significance' as a separate, non-mathematical claim it never proved.
seeds.source_citation: Iamblichus, Theologoumena arithmeticae (The Theology of Arithmetic), c. 300 CE - the mystical/numerological reading of figurate numbers and the Pythagorean tetractys, cited here as the SOURCE of the significance claim, not as mathematical evidence. The figurate identities themselves are the established facts (see nicomachus-sum-of-cubes, hexagonal-are-triangular, square-consecutive-triangulars); the 'sacred-geometry' reading is not established and has no promotion path.

seeds.title: 'Pell's equation' is a historical misnomer (Euler's misattribution)
seeds.statement: The name 'Pell's equation' for x^2 - N*y^2 = 1 is a well-documented historical misnomer. The equation was studied and essentially solved centuries earlier in India (Brahmagupta, 628 CE; Bhaskara II's chakravala, c. 1150 CE) and, in 17th-century Europe, was solved by William Brouncker in response to a challenge from Fermat (1657-58). Leonhard Euler, in his Elements of Algebra (1765) and earlier, mistakenly attributed the work to John Pell - who had little to do with it - and the name stuck. Some historians argue it should be the Brahmagupta-Bhaskara equation. M8 states this as context and must not present 'Pell' as an attribution of authorship.
seeds.source_citation: The 'Pell equation' name is a misattribution by Euler (Elements of Algebra, 1765), who is generally believed to have confused Brouncker's contributions (reported by Wallis) with John Pell's; the equation was solved far earlier by Brahmagupta (628) and Bhaskara II (chakravala, c. 1150), and in Europe by Brouncker (1657-58) at Fermat's challenge. MacTutor History of Mathematics, 'Pell's equation' (St Andrews); Weisstein, 'Pell Equation', Wolfram MathWorld.
